name: Hana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the pig manager on the Hollins farm, 350 sows, farrow to finish, plus about 280 hectares of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into the feed. My day starts at half five with the farrowing rooms, checking every sow that's due and every litter that's under a week old. Then it's feed, water lines, the weaners, and whatever's broken. In summer I'm on the combine at night as well, because there's only four of us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the farrowing. There's a moment when a sow settles and the piglets find the teat and you know you got it right, and I'm good at that, better than people twice my age. What wears me out is the pay. I'm running the whole unit for less than my mate gets stacking shelves, and I live with Lewis in a rented semi on Station Lane where the boiler's older than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like now. Nothing on this farm has an AI in it except the feed company's app, and I don't use that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone was going on about robots taking over and it turned out to be another gadget the feed reps try to sell you. Pigs still need someone who can tell a sick one by how it stands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix anything. My problem was never robots, it's that farm wages are rubbish and pig prices go up and down like a lift. A boring future still means I'm broke at the end of every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep at the unit, keep pushing Mr Hollins for a raise when the pig price is up, and maybe join the farmworkers' union properly instead of just meaning to. I've got about three weeks of money in the bank, so I don't do big plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, because calm for me still means counting coins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a raise. How does that conversation usually go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He agrees I'm worth more and then he shows me the pig price on his phone. Last time he gave me fifty pounds a month extra and a box of sausages at Christmas. I laughed, because what else do you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the feed company's app ever win you over in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It tells you what the pigs ate, and I already know what the pigs ate because I fed them. I'll use a tool when it saves me walking, not when it gives me another screen to look at.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, because AI turned out to be one more gadget the feed reps push. Pigs still need someone who can tell a sick one by how it stands.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but it changes nothing that matters to me. Low farm wages and a pig price that goes up and down like a lift are the real problems.
S0.do: Keeps running the pig unit as normal and pushes the owner for a raise when the pig price is up. Finally joins the farmworkers' union properly instead of just meaning to.
S0.feel: Calm, with a flat edge, because normal for her still means being short of money.
S0.quote: Pigs still need someone who can tell a sick one by how it stands.
S0.fieldNote: Hana's skill is obvious and she knows it; the farrowing story came with real pride. Her complaint in this calm world is pay, not technology. She dismisses AI tools quickly and on practical grounds, not ideology. Note the sausages at Christmas, which she tells as a joke but plainly resents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the feed rep's app gets clever, and someone sells Mr Hollins a robot for the muck. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who do the work should get a say in how these machines come in. If a robot cleans the pens, fine, but the money it saves shouldn't all go to the owner and the bank. That's what unions are for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think they'd come for the boring bits first, the pen washing and the feeding, and then someone would say a camera can spot a lame pig. That's the bit that's mine. I don't want to be the person who watches a screen tell me what I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my union card and get Dev and Sally on the farm to join too, so we can talk to Mr Hollins as a group. I'd agree to the pen-washing robot if it came, because my back would thank me. I would not go on some online course, I'd wait to see what actually turns up in the sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming in through the side door, one bit at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev. He's fifty-one, he does the washing and the muck and the tractor work, and he can't read very well. He'd be first, and nobody's going to retrain Dev on a computer. I'd fight for him before I'd fight for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what turns up. Some people would get ahead of it. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I've got ahead of something it cost money I didn't have. I bought a fancy pig-weighing thing once on a card and it broke in a month. I'd rather be the one who knows the pigs better than the machine does.

S1.say: I'd say the people doing the work should get a say in how machines come in. If a robot cleans the pens, the savings shouldn't all go to the owner and the bank.
S1.think: I think the machines would take the boring jobs first and then creep into spotting sick pigs, which is the part that's mine. I don't want to watch a screen tell me what I already know.
S1.do: Joins the farmworkers' union and gets two co-workers to join so they can talk to the owner as a group. Accepts a pen-washing robot for the sake of her back but refuses online courses and waits to see what arrives.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching change come in a bit at a time through the side door.
S1.quote: I'd fight for him before I'd fight for me.
S1.fieldNote: Her first thought in this scenario went to Dev, an older co-worker, not to herself. That fits her outlook, but it also lets her avoid planning for her own job. Her resistance to tools has a money story behind it: a weighing gadget bought on a credit card that broke. She will accept physical help but guards the judgement part of the job hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two harvests. I wouldn't even have the boiler fixed by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is being done to us by companies that have never smelled a pig shed. I'd say it at the union meeting and on the farming group chat, and I'd say the government needs to step in now, not after. Somebody has to pay for the people this throws out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm finished. A robot that can farrow sows and drive a combine at night doesn't need me, and Mr Hollins would buy it the day the bank said yes. With three weeks of money and a rented house, I'd have nothing to stand on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd cut everything: the phone contract, the takeaway on Fridays, the car insurance down to the minimum. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done. In the first year after, I'd be asking the council and the benefits office for whatever there is, and Lewis and I would probably move in with his mum in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight just thinking about handing back the keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't do anything except brace. In two years I can't save, I can't learn a new trade, I can barely finish a tax return. With longer I'd at least have a fighting chance, but two years is just watching the lorry come up the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. In this picture, would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. What's the point of learning to use the thing that's replacing me in two years? I'd rather spend the time with the sows I've got left and on getting the union to make some noise.

S2.say: I'd say this is being done to farmworkers by companies that have never smelled a pig shed. I'd say the government has to step in now and someone has to pay for the people it throws out.
S2.think: Privately I think I'm finished, because a robot that can farrow sows and drive a combine doesn't need me. With three weeks of money and a rented house, I'd have nothing to stand on.
S2.do: Cuts the phone contract, Friday takeaways and car insurance straight away and goes to every union meeting. Writes to her MP for the first time, then applies for council and benefit help and plans to move in with her partner's mother in town.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a tight chest at the thought of handing back the house keys.
S2.quote: Two years is just watching the lorry come up the lane.
S2.fieldNote: The short warning time turns Hana from a fighter into someone bracing for impact. She openly refuses to learn AI even here and calls it stubborn herself, which was striking. Her plans are all about defence: cutting costs, union noise, public help and family. She blames tech companies and expects government to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right. That's still fast, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, louder. Five years is enough time for the government to put proper rules in place, so there's no excuse. I'd be pushing for a law that farm owners can't sack long-standing workers for a robot without retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I might squeeze something out. I'd still lose the pig job, I'm sure of that, but I'd have time to save a bit and work out what's next. I just don't know what next looks like for someone who's only ever done pigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start putting fifty pounds a week aside, which means no holiday and no new boots. I'd get the union to push Mr Hollins for a written deal on redundancy pay. And I'd look at the HGV licence, because driving lorries is close to what I know and it's a course with an end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's like knowing a storm's coming on Thursday instead of now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an HGV licence, when robots might drive lorries too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, I hadn't thought that through. I suppose I picked it because I know what it is. If the robots drive the lorries too, then I don't know what's safe, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lewis the night you decided to start saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're not going to his sister's wedding abroad. He'd be gutted, because he's been looking forward to it for a year. But I'd say I'd rather miss one wedding than miss three months' rent.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to put proper rules in place, so there's no excuse. I'd push for a law that owners can't sack long-standing workers for a robot without retraining money.
S3.think: Privately I think I still lose the pig job, but I'd have time to save and work out what comes next. I honestly don't know what next looks like for someone who's only ever done pigs.
S3.do: Starts saving fifty pounds a week by skipping holidays and new boots, and gets the union to press for a written redundancy deal. Looks into an HGV lorry licence because it's a course with an end date.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to breathe, like knowing a storm is due on Thursday rather than today.
S3.quote: I'd rather miss one wedding than miss three months' rent.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she shifts from bracing to small, real plans, and saving appears for the first time. The HGV idea fell apart under one question and she admitted it plainly, which felt honest rather than defeated. Her politics turn into a specific demand: retraining money written into law. Skipping her partner's sister's wedding was the concrete cost she chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd want the farm unions and the colleges working out a plan for people like me now, while there's time. Not leaflets, actual places on courses that are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the one where I'd have a chance. I'd still hate it, because pigs are what I'm good at, but I could get out the right way instead of being thrown out. And if I'm being really honest, part of me thinks it won't happen and I'd waste the first few years waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year I'd probably do very little, if I'm truthful, apart from saving a bit and staying in the union. Maybe in year two or three I'd look at animal welfare inspection, because someone will still have to check the robots treat animals right. Lewis and I would put off buying anywhere until we could see where the work was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. Sad more than anything, because I love the sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do very little in the first year. Why, if you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough to tell yourself it's someone else's problem. Ask anyone in farming about the last thing that was coming in ten years. Half of it never came. I know that's how people get caught out, but it's how I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why animal welfare inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd trust a person to tell if a pig's in pain before I'd trust a camera. If there's one job I'd fight to keep human, that's it. And I'd be good at it, I can walk into a shed and smell if something's wrong.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift we mustn't waste, and the unions and colleges should plan for people like me now. I'd want paid places on courses, not leaflets.
S4.think: I think ten years gives me a real chance to leave the right way instead of being thrown out. Part of me also suspects I'd waste the first few years telling myself it won't happen.
S4.do: Saves a little and stays in the union in the first year, admitting she would do little else. Plans to look at animal welfare inspection in year two or three and puts off buying a home until the work picture is clear.
S4.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, and mostly sad at the thought of leaving the pig sheds.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to tell yourself it's someone else's problem.
S4.fieldNote: Hana predicted her own delay with unusual honesty: she expects to waste early years waiting. Her chosen future, welfare inspection, keeps the part of farming she cares about most, judging animals by eye and smell. For a resistant person, the long warning time doesn't speed her up; it gives her room to stall. The sadness here was about losing the sheds, not money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily, because I'd have no money and no time and I'd lose the house with the job. What would help is the government guaranteeing a wage while people retrain, a proper one, and farm owners being made to give notice and redundancy pay. And someone talking to Dev before they talk to the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about our jobs, but if machines run these sheds, who notices the sow that's off her food at three in the morning? I'd want that asked before anyone switches anything on.

headlineQuote: I'm running the whole unit for less than my mate gets stacking shelves
portrait: Hana Okafor is 27 and runs the pig unit on a farrow-to-finish farm with arable land, a job she is excellent at and paid poorly for. She rents a cold semi with her partner Lewis and has about three weeks of savings. She distrusts new tools, refuses to use AI even when it might help, and puts her faith in unions and government rules. In the calm worlds she worries about pay, not robots; in the fast AGI picture she braces for losing both job and home, while ten years gives her room to plan and, she admits, room to stall. Through it all she keeps coming back to an older co-worker, Dev, and to the welfare of the animals.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because with no savings and no time she would lose her job and her rented home together.
whatWouldHelp: A proper government-backed wage while people retrain, plus required notice and redundancy pay from farm owners. She also wants older workers like Dev looked after first.
